title: PEO Employee Benefits: Health, Workers' Comp & More | BBSI
summary: Learn how a PEO helps businesses offer health insurance, workers' compensation, retirement plans, and other employee benefits. Compare providers and evaluate your options before choosing a PEO.

Listen to the article: A Guide to Employee Benefits Through a PEO


8:54


Health insurance renewal rates rarely bring good news for small businesses, and 2027 looks no different. According to[KFF](https://www.kff.org/health-costs/how-much-and-why-premiums-are-going-up-for-small-businesses-in-2027/) , small-group insurers reported “a median proposed premium increase of 14% for next year.” Small employers absorb those hikes with little bargaining power, while also juggling the paperwork and compliance that come with offering benefits. No wonder more business owners are taking a hard look at PEOs as a way to improve employee benefits, manage rising healthcare costs, and reduce administrative burden. Here’s what we’ll cover:


- What Employee Benefits Can a PEO Provide? (and what it can’t)
- The types of services PEOs typically offer
- The role a PEO plays in managing your benefits
- A seven-point scorecard for comparing PEO companies
- The questions to ask before you sign anything


Let’s start with the basics.


## What Employee Benefits Can a PEO Provide?


A PEO can provide access to employee benefits and business insurance programs through a[co-employment](https://www.bbsi.com/partner-resources/what-co-employment-how-explain-smb-clients) relationship. These offerings often include health insurance, workers' compensation, retirement plans, and benefits administration services plus the administrative muscle to run them.


### So, what’s co-employment?


Co-employment is a contract that splits employer responsibilities between you and the PEO.[The PEO typically supports](https://www.bbsi.com/business-owner-resources/transforming-your-business-what-is-a-peo) things like payroll administration, benefits management, and compliance while you keep running the business: the day-to-day calls, the team dynamics, the culture, and who gets the good parking spot. You’re still the boss; you’ve just got backup.


Here’s where business owners get tripped up. PEO programs aren’t a policy you pull off a shelf. It’s a bundle: the coverage itself, plus the people and systems that manage it. To size up any PEO, you need to look hard at both halves. Let’s start with the coverage.


## What Employee Benefits and Insurance Programs Can You Access Through a PEO?


Most PEOs offer some combination of:


- Medical, dental, and vision coverage
- Life and disability insurance
- [Voluntary and supplemental plans](https://www.bbsi.com/business-owner-resources/closing-the-gap-protection-for-lifes-unexpected-events) (think accident or critical illness coverage)
- Flexible spending accounts (FSAs) and[health savings accounts (HSAs)](https://www.bbsi.com/business-owner-resources/how-hsas-create-value-for-highly-compensated-employees)
- Retirement plans, often through a multiple-employer 401(k)
- Workers’ compensation


The coverage access a PEO provides matters because health coverage is expensive, and it isn’t getting cheaper anytime soon. According to[KFF’s 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey](https://www.kff.org/health-costs/2025-employer-health-benefits-survey/) , “Annual premiums for employer-sponsored family health coverage reached $26,993 this year,” a 6% increase from the year before. While a 15-person shop may not have the bargaining power to bring that number down, a PEO has more muscle.


How PEO insurance coverage is set up varies from PEO to PEO. Some offer access to PEO-sponsored health plans, others set up plans at the individual client level, and some let you[keep the plan you already have](https://www.bbsi.com/business-owner-resources/peo-vs-open-market-health-insurance) while you use their other services. Offerings also vary by state, so ask what’s actually available where your employees live and work, not just what’s on the plan brochure.


## What Role Does a PEO Play in Managing Employee Benefits?


Coverage is only half the bundle. The other half is the work, and there’s a lot of it. A good PEO typically covers three areas:


### Plan Administration


This means guidance on choosing plans, managing enrollment, and processing life events like marriages and new babies. It also means managing payroll deductions and reconciling carrier bills. It’s the tedious stuff that quickly eats away at your Tuesday afternoons.


### Compliance Support


Many PEOs help with[benefits compliance](https://www.bbsi.com/business-owner-resources/whats-changing-in-2026-hr-benefits-compliance-at-a-glance) , such as Affordable Care Act (ACA) reporting on Forms 1094 and 1095, COBRA administration, and ERISA plan documents. But “compliance support” isn’t a standard package. One PEO may track ACA eligibility across your whole workforce, while another files forms only for employees enrolled in its health plan. Your contract spells out who’s on the hook for what, so read it closely.


### Employee Support & Workers’ Comp


Many PEOs offer pay-as-you-go workers’ comp, which calculates premiums on actual, real-time payroll instead of an upfront estimate that’s subject to change annually. Claims management and safety support may be included, too, depending on the provider. Someone has to field employee questions like, “Why was my claim denied?” Ideally, that someone isn’t you.


Now that you know what’s in the bundle, the real question is how to tell the best PEO companies apart.


## How Should You Evaluate PEO Companies on Insurance and Benefits?


You’ve got options, and lots of them. According to[NAPEO](https://napeo.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/PEOIndustryFootprint_WhitePaper2026.pdf) , 502 PEOs were operating at the end of 2025, but they are not interchangeable. Here’s a seven-point scorecard for comparing PEO companies on insurance and benefits. We recommend asking these questions at every sales call.


1. **Plan options and carriers.** A great plan in Texas does nothing for your team in Oregon.
*Ask:* Which carriers, networks, and plan tiers are available in the states where my employees work?
2. **Benefit model and flexibility.** Some PEOs require you to join their health plan. Others don’t.
*Ask:* Is this a PEO-sponsored plan or a client-level plan? Is joining required? Can I keep my current plan or broker?
3. **Pricing transparency.** Bundled pricing may mask what you’re paying for coverage.
*Ask:* How are admin fees charged? As a percentage of payroll, per employee, or bundled? Are premiums itemized separately?
4. **Renewal history.** A sweet first-year rate means very little if year two gives you whiplash.
*Ask:* What have average renewal rates looked like over the past three years, and how is my renewal rate set?
5. **Compliance responsibility.** “We handle compliance” is a slogan, not a contract.
*Ask:* Which ACA, COBRA, and ERISA tasks does the PEO support, and which stay with me? Does ACA support include eligibility tracking, or just Forms 1094 and 1095?
6. [Workers’ comp handling](https://www.bbsi.com/workers-comp) **.** This affects your cash flow and how claims get handled.
*Ask:* Is it pay-as-you-go or deposit-and-audit? Who manages claims? Can I keep my own carrier?
7. **Service model.** When an employee’s claim goes sideways, somebody has to pick up the phone.
*Ask:* Will I have a dedicated contact and a local team, or a general call center?


Finally, check credentials. ESAC accreditation, SOC 1 certification, an independent board, and audited financials each speak to a PEO’s financial stability and business practices. Verify every claim on the issuer’s public lookup rather than taking the sales deck’s word for it.


## What Should You Ask Before Signing a PEO Agreement?


Before you sign, nail down two things:


**1. Exit Terms**


Think of exit terms as a prenup. Ask how much notice you’ll need to give to terminate your contract, what happens to employees’ health coverage if you exit mid-year, and how COBRA and 401(k) accounts are handled on the way out.


**2. Contract Scope**


Get a written breakdown of which employer responsibilities move to the PEO and which stay with you. If it isn’t on paper, you should assume it’s still yours.


Then watch for these red flags:


- Bundled pricing the PEO won’t break out
- Fuzzy, hand-wavy answers about renewal history
- Pressure to join the health plan before you’ve seen the options in your state
- Credentials you can’t verify


A PEO that answers all of this clearly, without squirming, is one worth a serious look.

## Quick Summary


PEO services provide bundle solutions for employee benefits and business coverage, plus the administration that comes with it, which a PEO provides through co-employment. This guide explains what coverage PEOs typically offer and what role they play in managing benefits and compliance. It also gives business owners a seven-point scorecard for comparing PEO companies before they sign.


---


## PEO Coverage FAQs


##### Is PEO coverage cheaper than buying coverage on my own?


It can be, because PEOs may provide access to PEO-sponsored health plans with improved plan options and pricing. Results vary by location, workforce, and claims history, so be sure to compare actual quotes.


##### Do I have to use a PEO’s health plan?


Not always. Some PEOs require it, while others let you keep your existing plan and still use their payroll and HR services.


##### What happens to employee coverage if I leave a PEO?


That depends on your contract and how the PEO structures its plans. Before you sign, ask about notice periods, mid-year transitions, and how COBRA is handled.
